paras: The killing of George Hathaway was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a white man, Martin Murphy, at a Black dance in Carlisle, Kentucky, on the night of September 27, 1882. Hathaway died on October 2, and Murphy escaped while armed men searched for him. A national wire brief retold the case as a white man defying a ban on white dancers, and it circulated from Delaware to Montana.

According to the Carlisle column of the Bourbon News, Murphy and several other white men attended the "colored fair hops" on Wednesday night. The same paper described Murphy as "a very small man, aged 22," and the foreman in Hanley's carpenter shop.

During the dance Hathaway, described as "a man of color," stepped on Murphy's toes and apologized. Murphy left, came back a few minutes later, and shot Hathaway twice in the bowels; a stray shot hit Charlie Mower, a fireman on the K. C. road, in the foot. Murphy fled the house to a cornfield that white and Black pursuers surrounded, but he got away. A dispatch dated Carlisle, September 28, reported only that Murphy "shot and killed" George Hathaway at a dance the night before.

On Saturday night, September 30, a squad of "Carlisle boys" armed with shotguns and corn knives came to Millersburg looking for Murphy. The Maysville Evening Bulletin reported that "the negro boy, Hathaway" died on Monday, October 2. No report of Murphy's arrest, an inquest, or a trial appears in the coverage.

Kentucky papers treated the killing briefly and sometimes as a joke: a Lexington Transcript item reprinted in the Bourbon News said a white man shot a Black man "for stepping on his foot" and added that "The negro had to step somewhere." The Arkansaw Traveler built a humor piece about corns around the case, yet called Murphy "the murderer" and predicted that Kentucky courts would "deal gently" with him.

A different version spread through the wire, headed "A White Man in the Wrong Place" in the Wilmington Daily Republican on October 7. It said a notice at the "negro ball" read "No white persons allowed to dance," that Murphy "defiantly waltzed with a black belle," and that he shot "Nick Hathaway, a floor manager," who interfered, after which firing wounded four men. The brief ran in Wheeling, Dallas, Memphis, Ohio, Montana and South Carolina papers through early November, one of them giving the name as "Dick Hathaway," and none reported that Hathaway had died.

The local column and the Carlisle dispatch place the shooting on Wednesday night, while the Lexington Transcript said Thursday. The Kentucky and Carlisle reports name the victim George and give a stepped-on foot as the cause, while the later wire brief names him Nick and gives the posted ban as the cause; the local accounts are earlier and closer to the scene.

framing.detail: The Lexington Transcript, reprinted in the Bourbon News, joked that 'The negro had to step somewhere'.

The Maysville Bulletin and Evening Critic gave one-line notices of the shooting and death.
